name: Guard Pulling Strategy
keyCorrections: If you keep landing flat on your back: you are not sitting to one hip. Focus on sitting to your outside hip while keeping the inside leg active
If the opponent passes immediately after you pull: your distance was wrong or you lost the grip. Pull closer and maintain the grip until you establish guard
If the opponent circles out before you pull: you did not create enough angle. Circle further off the center line before sitting
description: Pull guard with intent: grip and angle first, then seated, shin-to-shin, K-guard, or wrestle-up plan. A guard pull is an offensive entry that should lead directly to one of your strongest guard systems.
shortInstruction: Establish a grip (collar tie or wrist control), create an angle off the center line, sit back to one hip, and enter your chosen guard (seated, shin-to-shin, K-guard) immediately. Pulling guard without a plan is conceding position.
summary: Guard pulling should be an offensive transition, not a defensive retreat. The sequence is: establish a dominant grip → create an angle by circling or pummeling → control the distance by maintaining the grip → sit back with control → enter directly into your best guard system. A well-executed guard pull arrives in a scoring guard (not flat on your back) with grips already established and the opponent off-balance.
whyItWorks: Establishing a grip before pulling ensures you control the distance — the opponent cannot back away or circle to side control
Creating an angle (stepping off the center line) forces the opponent to re-align, giving you the opening to pull without being passed
Pulling to a specific guard system (seated, shin-to-shin, K-guard) rather than a generic closed guard gives you an immediate offensive plan
A controlled pull prevents the opponent from immediately scoring a pass or takedown on your landing
commonMistakes: Pulling guard without any grip — the opponent can immediately disengage or circle to side control
Sitting back straight (both hips down) instead of sitting to one hip — this lands you flat, giving them an immediate pass opportunity
Pulling guard too far away — if there is a 3-foot gap when you sit, the opponent can disengage and reset
Forgetting to maintain the grip after pulling — the grip is what keeps them in your guard and prevents them from standing up and passing
coachingCues: Land on one hip, not flat
Pull to a guard, not to the floor
safetySummary: Do not sit back explosively if your foot is caught between the opponent's legs — this can cause ankle or knee injury
When pulling guard in competition, be aware of slam rules — in some rule sets, the opponent can lift and slam you if you pull guard without grips
Practice guard pulling with a resisting partner at controlled speed before using it live — a bad guard pull can land you in side control immediately

systemLogic.corePrinciple: Guard pulling follows a four-step sequence: Grip → Angle → Sit → Enter Guard System

decisionTree.action: establish your strongest guard grip before pulling. If pulling to shin-to-shin: collar tie + wrist control. If pulling to K-guard: collar tie + sleeve grip. If pulling to seated guard: two-on-one wrist control or collar tie
step off the center line at a 30-45 degree angle. If you pull straight at them, they can drive forward into side control. An angle forces them to re-align their hips, creating the entry window

lower your hips to the mat by sitting to your outside hip (not both hips at once). Keep your inside leg active (posted foot or shin-to-shin connection) to prevent them from stepping into the guard pass

immediately transition to your best guard from the landing position. If you pulled to shin-to-shin: enter single leg X or X-guard. If you pulled to seated: enter K-guard, DLR, or collar-sleeve. If you pulled to closed guard: break their posture immediately
against a standing passer → seated guard. Against a kneeling passer → shin-to-shin. Against pressure passer → K-guard or butterfly

moneyDetails: A good guard pull is the foundation of your entire guard game — it determines whether you start the guard sequence in a strong or weak position
Competition guard pulling is a strategic decision — pulling guard to enter your best attack system is often better than wrestling for a takedown
Mastering guard pulling allows you to dictate where the match starts — you choose the guard system, not the opponent
fixItFast: If the opponent is rushing you as you try to pull: use a collar tie to post on their head and circle behind their rush before pulling
If you keep getting passed during the pull: you are not controlling their far leg. Keep your foot on their far hip as you sit to prevent the knee cut
If the opponent disengages after you pull: use a wrestle-up to stand and re-engage rather than sitting and waiting
